problem: Prior audio-visual navigation agents use a staged pipeline (convolution or attention fusion, then a GRU for sequence modeling, then RL). This causes redundant information processing and inconsistent information transfer between fusion and GRU, and limits efficiency and generalization to unheard sounds.
motivation: Audio-goal navigation (e.g. locating a call for help, a gas alarm or running water) needs both a high success rate and fast arrival. Early attention fusion already models some long-range dependencies implicitly, so a following GRU duplicates that work. GRUs are also sequential and prone to information decay. The paper merges fusion and sequence modeling into one module.
key_idea: Replace the separate feature-fusion and GRU modules with a single transformer-style decoder that cross-attends over the multimodal sequence, and concatenate its output back with the initial multimodal sequence at each iteration (multi-level residuals).
insight: The ablations show the encoder (EN) and patch embedding (PE) matter most. On Replica Unheard SPL, w/o EN gives 23.4 and w/o PE 35.6, against 51.9 for the full model. Removing the iterative residual concatenation (RT) gives a smaller but consistent drop (46.1 SPL Unheard, 84.4 Heard). The gain over CNN+GRU and SelfAttention+GRU (FSAAVN) suggests that unified attention with residual re-injection of the initial sequence helps generalization to unheard sounds. The paper gives no analysis of compute cost or of whether the GRU removal alone is responsible.
method: Patch embedding + encoder: audio and visual observations are embedded as patch sequences, concatenated, and passed through self-attention to form the Initial Multimodal Sequence.
Cross-attention decoder: a query sequence Q attends over the multimodal sequence E_t as key/value using multi-head attention, extracting navigation cues.

Iterative residual concatenation (RT): E_{t+1}=Concat(Decoder(E_t),E_t), so the initial sequence is re-injected into each successive decoder step (external residuals among encoders, plus internal residuals in encoder and decoder).
Unified module: this block replaces both the feature-fusion and GRU stages.
Actor-critic policy: the output feeds an actor-critic network trained with RL (discount 0.99, Adam, 500-step episodes).

setting.backbone: IRCAM transformer-style encoder-decoder with patch embedding + actor-critic (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: RL in SoundSpaces on Replica (80k agent steps, lr 1e-4) and Matterport3D (100k agent steps, lr 4e-5); no extra data
setting.action_space: low-level discrete actions (SoundSpaces: move forward, turn left/right, stop)

numbers_note: The paper does not name the split (heard/unheard sound settings only); 'test' is assumed. Benchmark is the SoundSpaces audio-goal task on Replica and Matterport3D.
results: IRCAM beats ORAN, the strongest baseline, on Replica: Unheard SPL 51.9 vs 46.7, Heard SPL 89.9 vs 84.2. On Matterport3D it beats AV-WaN by 8.4 SPL on Heard and 11.5 SPL on Unheard. Replica Heard SR (97.6) is below AV-WaN's 98.7. It also beats CNN+GRU (SoundSpaces) and SelfAttention+GRU (FSAAVN) on SPL.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation (SoundSpaces on Replica and Matterport3D), with no real-robot tests and no compute or latency comparison.
Replica Heard SR is not the best (97.6 vs AV-WaN 98.7). Unheard performance is still far below Heard (Replica SR 64.4 vs 97.6).
The method description is loose: the equations swap the audio/visual input labels, the meaning of the iterative decoder is unclear, and there are no multi-seed results.
